slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
slides.eyebrow: Urinalysis · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Urine (clean-catch sample; 24-hour collection in some cases)

What it is used for: A urinalysis may include a visual check, tests for certain chemicals and a microscopic exam; the chemical part checks substances such as protein, glucose, ketones, bilirubin, urobilinogen and nitrites, and dipstick (test strip) methods can be used. Urinalysis is used to check general health, including the urinary tract and kidneys, and helps diagnose kidney and liver problems.

Urine ketones are used to monitor people more likely to develop high ketone levels, such as those with diabetes, long-lasting vomiting or diarrhea, alcohol use disorder, eating disorders or starvation, certain digestive diseases, a low-carbohydrate (“keto”) diet, prolonged very hard exercise, or pregnancy.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
slides.eyebrow: Urinalysis · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Normally urine contains very little protein, because tiny kidney filters stop large protein molecules from passing into urine. High urine protein over time may be the first sign that kidney disease or another condition has damaged these filters, so the test can help find kidney damage early.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
bullets: High: High urine protein can be temporary, for example due to strenuous exercise, dehydration, diet, stress or pregnancy, so repeat testing may be needed. Protein that stays high is likely a sign of kidney disease or kidney damage, and more tests are needed to find the cause.

High: Normally urine contains little or no glucose because the kidneys return it to the blood. More glucose than normal may reflect high blood glucose (diabetes is the most common cause) or, rarely, a kidney condition such as renal glycosuria or Fanconi syndrome, in which glucose is removed even when blood glucose is normal. Pregnancy and gestational diabetes are also listed.
High: Many bacteria that cause urinary tract infections (UTIs) change nitrates, a normal chemical in urine, into nitrites, so nitrites in urine usually mean a UTI.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
bullets: High: When cells cannot get enough glucose, the body breaks down fat for energy, producing ketones. Some ketones in urine are normal, but high levels may indicate ketoacidosis, most commonly diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a medical emergency that often develops quickly and can be life-threatening.

High: Bilirubin is normally not found in urine. Its presence (bilirubinuria) may be a sign of liver disease, such as hepatitis or cirrhosis, or of a blockage in the bile ducts; it can be an early sign of liver damage and may appear before symptoms do.

High: Normal urine contains some urobilinogen, which helpful gut bacteria make from bilirubin in bile. A higher-than-normal level may be a sign of hepatitis, cirrhosis, liver damage due to medicines or hemolytic anemia.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
bullets: Low: Too little or no urobilinogen may be a sign of a blockage in the ducts that carry bile from the liver or gallbladder to the intestines, a blockage of blood flow through the liver, or a problem with liver function.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
bullets: Pre-analytics: Because the amount of protein and other substances in urine varies during the day, a 24-hour urine collection may give more complete results.

The sample is usually collected by the clean-catch method: after washing hands and cleaning the genital area, the first few seconds of urine go into the toilet and the rest is collected in the container without touching its inside, so that germs from the skin do not get into the sample. Bleeding hemorrhoids or a menstrual period should be reported before the test.

Fasting may be required before a urine ketone test or when other urine or blood tests are ordered. Some medicines may need to be stopped, but only on the provider’s instruction; all medicines being taken should be reported.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
bullets: Urine for routine analysis is examined within 1 hour of collection, and the pH must also be tested within 1 hour. If testing is delayed, keep the sample refrigerated until it is analysed.

What changes when urine stands: per the WHO table, glucose falls within about 2 hours both at room temperature and at 4–8 °C (bacteria consume it), and pH rises as ammonium forms, so the urine turns alkaline. The textbook lists the same changes and stresses falsely low glucose after a delay.
Urine protein is more stable: the WHO table gives 1 day at room temperature, 7 days at 4–8 °C and 1 month at −20 °C.
Interferences: Certain medicines, vitamin C and eating a large meal may affect urine glucose results.
Certain medicines and supplements can affect urine bilirubin and urobilinogen results, so everything being taken should be reported.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
bullets: Bilirubin breaks down in light: the textbook says fresh urine must be shielded from sunlight and fluorescent light, because bilirubin oxidises to biliverdin, which the strip does not detect (false negative). The WHO document likewise requires darkness for serum bilirubin stored over 8 hours; it gives no separate time for urine.
Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) can affect the urine glucose result; the textbook lists it as a substance that lowers strip sensitivity and gives a false-negative result.

Limitations: Urine glucose testing is less accurate than blood glucose testing, so blood tests are now more commonly used to diagnose and monitor diabetes. A normal urine glucose does not exclude diabetes, because urine glucose can be normal while blood glucose is high, and a urine glucose test alone cannot diagnose any condition.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
bullets: A negative nitrite test does not exclude infection, because some bacteria do not change nitrates into nitrites; results for white blood cells in urine are also considered. Home UTI test strips may miss an infection, and a urine culture shows how much and what type of bacteria are present.
Ketone results may be a number or reported as a “small”, “moderate” or “large” amount, and normal results can vary with diet, activity level and other factors.
Urine bilirubin is only one measure of liver health, and a urobilinogen test alone cannot diagnose a specific condition; abnormal results may lead to further tests such as a liver panel.

slides.title: Stool examination (coprology)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Stool (clean, dry container; no urine, water or toilet paper)  ·  Units: g/24 h

What it is used for: Stool tests look for blood, bacteria, parasites or signs of disease — for example, when looking for the cause of diarrhea. Finding white blood cells on microscopy helps tell whether diarrhea is due to inflammation in the gut.

Physiology: The normal brown colour of stool comes from bile salts released by the liver. Absorbing fat needs bile, pancreatic enzymes and a normal small intestine; when absorption fails, stool fat rises (steatorrhea).

slides.title: Stool examination (coprology)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Interpreting the result · 1/2
bullets: Pale or clay-coloured stool may point to a problem in the biliary system: a liver infection that reduces bile production, or blocked bile flow out of the liver. Jaundice and dark urine often occur with it.

Black, tarry stool (melena) most often means bleeding in the upper GI tract — oesophagus, stomach or first part of the small intestine; the blood darkens as it is digested. Red, fresh blood in stool most often comes from the lower GI tract (colon, rectum or anus).

White blood cells in stool mean there is inflammation in the digestive tract. This helps rule out viral infections, certain bacteria and most parasites. Causes of inflammatory diarrhea include some bacterial infections (C. difficile, Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter), inflammatory bowel disease and Entamoeba histolytica; further tests show the exact cause.

slides.title: Stool examination (coprology)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Interpreting the result · 2/2
bullets: Stool fat is checked under a microscope on a single sample, or measured in all stool collected over 24 hours (sometimes 3 days). MedlinePlus gives less than 7 g of fat per 24 hours as normal for the quantitative test. Reduced fat absorption occurs with celiac disease, chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, Crohn disease, biliary strictures or gallstones, and other conditions.

A Gram-stained stool smear is read for the colour, size and shape of bacteria. A normal result shows only the usual ("friendly") gut bacteria. An abnormal result means an intestinal infection may be present; stool culture and other tests help find the cause.

slides.title: Stool examination (coprology)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/2
bullets: Pre-analytics: Stool is caught in a clean, dry container or on special paper or plastic wrap over the toilet; never take the sample from toilet water, and keep urine, water and toilet paper out. Label the container with name, date and time, close it tightly and wash hands with soap. If it cannot be returned right away, refrigerate it. For children in diapers, plastic wrap is placed inside the diaper.
Before a quantitative fat test, eat a normal diet with about 100 g of fat a day for 3 days, then collect all stool over 24 hours (sometimes 3 days) in the containers provided.

Interferences: Black stool can also come from black licorice, blueberries, blood sausage, iron pills, activated charcoal or bismuth medicines rather than blood; beets and red-coloured foods can make stool look reddish. In these cases the stool is tested chemically for blood.

slides.title: Stool examination (coprology)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/2
bullets: Enemas, laxatives, mineral oil and too little dietary fat before and during collection interfere with the fat test.

Limitations: A negative result cannot rule out inflammation: white cells do not last long in stool and may break apart before testing. The test cannot name the exact cause of diarrhea; when the picture is unclear, a stool calprotectin test may be ordered.

rows: G1 ≥90; G2 60–89; G3a 45–59; G3b 30–44; G4 15–29; G5 <15 (if persisting >3 months) mL/min/1.73 m²

slides.title: A patient with UTI symptoms has a negative urine nitrite test. Which interpretation follows the source?
options: A negative nitrite fully rules out a UTI
Infection is still possible because some bacteria do not change nitrates into nitrites; white blood cell results are also considered
A negative nitrite indicates kidney disease
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. The source describes exactly this limitation and the need to look at white blood cells in urine.

Basis: The nitrite test relies on bacteria changing nitrates into nitrites; bacteria that do not do this give a negative result despite infection.

slides.title: A large amount of protein is found in the urine of a person who ran a marathon the day before. Which approach follows the source?
options: Diagnose chronic kidney disease from this single result, because a large amount of protein in urine is never a temporary finding
Ignore it, because protein in urine after exercise is always harmless and needs no follow-up
Recognize that strenuous exercise can raise urine protein for a short time and check on repeat testing whether it persists
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. The source lists strenuous exercise as a cause of a short-term rise and suggests repeat urinalysis to see whether protein stays high.

Basis: Urine protein can rise temporarily; it is persistently high protein that points to kidney disease.

Theory of urine formation?
bullets: 1. Urine is formed in the nephron: filtration in the glomeruli (primary urine – protein-free ultrafiltrate of plasma, ~180 L per day), reabsorption and secretion in the tubules, concentration in the collecting ducts.
2. Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is the main indicator of kidney function; in practice eGFR is calculated from creatinine (and cystatin C).

3. Proximal tubule: glucose, amino acids, bicarbonate, Na and most of the water are reabsorbed; loop of Henle – concentration gradient via the countercurrent mechanism; distal tubule and collecting ducts – final regulation under aldosterone (Na/K) and ADH (water).
4. Laboratory reflection: glucosuria (if filtered glucose exceeds reabsorption capacity), proteinuria (glomerular or tubular damage), urine density/osmolality (concentrating ability).
5. Kidney disease is classified by KDIGO by eGFR (G1–G5) and albuminuria (A1–A3).

slides.title: Examining the physical and chemical properties of urine?
bullets: 1. Physical properties: amount (in adults ~600–2000 mL/day), color (bilirubin, blood, hemoglobin/myoglobin, drugs), clarity (turbidity – salts, leukocytes, bacteria, mucus), odor, relative density (1.002–1.035; urinometer, refractometer or test strip) – renal concentrating ability.

2. Chemical examination – test strips: pH (4.5–8), protein (mainly albumin; alkaline pH – false positive), glucose (when the reabsorption threshold is exceeded), ketones (acetoacetate/acetone, β-hydroxybutyrate is not detected), blood (erythrocytes, hemoglobin, myoglobin – peroxidase activity), leukocyte esterase, nitrites (some bacteria), bilirubin, urobilinogen.
3. Interferences: ascorbate (false negative blood, glucose, nitrite, leukocyte esterase), concentrated or dilute urine, drugs (phenazopyridine).

slides.title: Examining the physical and chemical properties of urine?
bullets: 4. Confirmatory tests: for protein – sulfosalicylic acid (all proteins) and quantitative UPCR/ACR, for blood – microscopy, glucose and ketones in blood.
5. Preanalytics: midstream, morning urine, analysis within 1 hour or storage at 4 °C.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy?
bullets: 1. Preparation: 5–12 mL of well-mixed fresh urine, centrifuged at ~400×g for 5 minutes, resuspended in a standard volume; under a coverslip at low (×100) and high (×400) magnification; phase contrast/staining, polarization for crystals.

2. Organized elements: erythrocytes (normal 0–5/field; dysmorphic erythrocytes and acanthocytes – glomerular source), leukocytes (0–5; many – infection, inflammation), epithelium (squamous, transitional, renal tubular), casts.

3. Casts: hyaline (a few are normal; concentrated urine, exertion), erythrocyte (glomerulonephritis, vasculitis), leukocyte (pyelonephritis, interstitial nephritis), granular (tubular damage), waxy (severe CKD), fatty (nephrotic syndrome).
4. Unorganized elements: crystals (oxalates, urates, uric acid, triple phosphates – infection; cystine – cystinuria), bacteria, fungi, trichomonads, sperm.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy?
bullets: 5. Automated urine particle analyzers (flow cytometry, digital imaging) – screening; abnormal results are confirmed by microscopy; the result is standardized per unit volume (/µL).
